title: Decisions, Decisions
coreMove: Break one overloaded choice into options, branches, consequences, and visible unknowns so each path can be compared without pretending certainty exists.
sourcePressure: The source support centers on decision trees as a way to tame complexity and make uncertainty discussable.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Thinking a decision tree is valuable because it makes the future precise, rather than because it makes the remaining ambiguity visible.

sourceAnchors.name: decision tree
sourceAnchors.detail: the source confirms the chapter anchor as breaking a choice into branches, outcomes, and consequences instead of one blurred feeling
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The tree does not remove the fog; it cuts the fog into paths you can name.

tryThisNow: Make a pros and cons list

exampleSpecs.domain: Thomas, a regional train dispatcher choosing between holding a connection or keeping the line on schedule during a signal fault
exampleSpecs.stakes: one choice strands passengers, the other cascades delays across the network
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Thomas draws three branches on the incident pad, marks which delay is known and which passenger impact is uncertain, then calls the control room
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 6:43 p.m., Thomas hears the signal alarm and reaches for the incident pad

exampleSpecs.domain: Camille, a children’s hospital fundraiser deciding whether to run a gala, a smaller donor dinner, or a digital campaign
exampleSpecs.audience: nonprofit leaders choosing under resource uncertainty
exampleSpecs.stakes: staff capacity and donor trust are limited before year end
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Camille separates each fundraising option into cost, staff-load, and donor-risk branches instead of labeling the gala “best” because it is familiar
exampleSpecs.firstImage: folded banquet linens sit beside a half-finished donor-call sheet
mustAvoid: generic nonprofit metric example from chapter 2

exampleSpecs.domain: Sam, a software reliability engineer deciding whether to patch, roll back, or leave a degraded release while customer traffic is high
exampleSpecs.audience: technical readers managing uncertainty without fake precision
exampleSpecs.stakes: each option carries outage, data, and trust consequences
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sam writes the three options on the war-room glass, adds unknowns under each one, and stops the team from voting on mood alone
exampleSpecs.firstImage: the war-room glass squeaks as the marker hits the word rollback

exampleSpecs.domain: Marta, a tenant organizer choosing whether to accept a partial repair promise, escalate publicly, or wait for legal aid
exampleSpecs.audience: civic readers facing choices with power imbalance
exampleSpecs.stakes: tenants need heat fixed but could lose leverage if they choose the wrong path
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Marta asks the room to stop arguing labels and put likely landlord responses under each path
exampleSpecs.firstImage: “Which branch gets the heat fixed, and which one only feels stronger?”

exampleSpecs.domain: Yusuf, a documentary editor deciding whether to cut a beloved scene that slows the final act
exampleSpecs.audience: creative workers whose choices bundle taste, pacing, and stakeholder risk
exampleSpecs.stakes: the festival cut could become either sharper or flatter
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Yusuf turns one painful creative feeling into branches for pacing, character clarity, and director trust, then tests two cuts
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Yusuf six rough cuts to see the scene was three different decisions hiding in one ache

exampleSpecs.domain: Giulia, a graduate researcher deciding whether to change methods after an early dataset comes back messy
exampleSpecs.audience: researchers and analysts dealing with unresolved ambiguity
exampleSpecs.stakes: switching too fast wastes months, staying too long can bury the project
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Giulia marks which unknowns belong to sampling, method design, and time budget before choosing the next week’s test
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You can stare at a messy dataset for an hour and still not know which problem it is

tryThisNowSpec: Write one hard choice as three branches. Under each branch, add one consequence you can see and one unknown you must not pretend away.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

skillTargets: identify the chapter-specific model in a fresh scenario for Decisions, Decisions
choose the visible action that performs the core move rather than naming the concept
explain the failure mode that appears when the model is used generically
evaluate tradeoffs and limits without sliding into certainty, cynicism, or manipulation

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'
